content:
If \(n<6\), the two lightest and four heaviest overlap. For \(n=5\), let weights be \(a\le b\le c\le d\le e\). Then
\[
a+b=80,\quad b+c+d+e=200,
\]
so total
\[
a+b+c+d+e = a+200=500,
\]
giving \(a=300\), impossible since \(a+b=80\). Thus \(n\ge 6\), so the groups are disjoint.

Let \(m=n-6\) be the number of remaining kittens. Then
\[
m\text{ kittens weigh }500-80-200=220\text{ g}.
\]
Since the two lightest sum to \(80\), the second-lightest weighs at least \(40\), so each middle kitten weighs at least \(40\). Also the four heaviest average \(200/4=50\), so their lightest weighs at most \(50\), and each middle kitten weighs at most \(50\). Hence
\[
40m\le 220\le 50m.
\]
Thus \(4.4\le m\le 5.5\), so \(m=5\). Therefore
\[
n=m+6=11.
\]

\[
\boxed{11}
\]
